about.title: Glendora Slip & Fall Claims
about.longDescription: Glendora's mix of older downtown storefronts along Route 66, shopping centers near Grand Avenue, and residential complexes tucked below the foothills means property conditions vary widely across town. A spill left unattended in a grocery aisle, a broken step at an apartment building, or uneven pavement in a parking lot can all lead to serious falls. California law doesn't automatically hold a property owner responsible just because someone got hurt on their premises — you generally need to show the owner knew, or reasonably should have known, about the hazard and didn't fix it or warn people about it. That's why documentation matters so much: photos of the hazard, witness names, and store surveillance footage can make or break a claim before it disappears or gets deleted. LawProactive doesn't practice law ourselves; we simply connect Glendora residents hurt in falls with an independent attorney who can evaluate the notice issue, gather evidence, and explain your options, all on a contingency basis so there's no upfront cost.

whyChoose.title: Why Notice and Evidence Matter in Glendora Falls

items.title: Proving the Owner Knew or Should Have Known
items.desc: California premises liability claims hinge on showing the property owner had notice of the hazard and failed to address it. An attorney can help identify inspection logs, maintenance records, or prior complaints that establish this notice.

items.title: Racing Against Deleted Surveillance Footage
items.desc: Many Glendora businesses overwrite security camera footage within days or weeks. Acting quickly to request preservation of that video can be the difference between a supported claim and one with no visual evidence.

items.title: Understanding Comparative Fault Before It's Used Against You
items.desc: California applies pure comparative fault, meaning your recovery can be reduced but not eliminated if you're found partly responsible for the fall. An attorney can push back on unfair blame while your case is built.

items.question: I fell at a store near Grand Avenue — do I automatically have a case?
items.answer: Not automatically. You generally need to show the store knew or should have known about the hazard, like a spill or debris, and didn't fix it or warn customers in time. An attorney can review the specific circumstances, including any surveillance footage or witness accounts, to see if that notice requirement is met.

items.question: How long do I have to file a premises liability claim in Glendora?
items.answer: In most cases, California gives you two years from the date of the fall to file a lawsuit. If the property involved is owned by a government entity, such as a city building or public sidewalk, the deadline is much shorter and requires an earlier claim process. It's best to get evidence and advice sooner rather than later.

items.question: What if I was partly at fault for not seeing the hazard?
items.answer: California follows pure comparative fault, so being partially responsible doesn't bar you from recovery — it just may reduce the amount. For example, if you were distracted but the hazard was also unmarked and unreasonably left in place, both factors get weighed. An attorney can help make sure the fault assigned to you is fair and supported by evidence.
